title: Client Communication in English
subtitle: Write to foreign clients without sounding apologetic
summary: The writing side of freelancing with foreign clients: the update nobody has to chase, saying no to extra work, sending bad news the day you learn it, asking a question that actually gets answered, and handling a client who is unhappy. Twelve lessons on what your English is being judged on, which is not your grammar.
description: This is not a grammar course. This course assumes your English already works well enough to do the job; what costs you clients is register and structure. Filipino freelancers writing to clients in the US, Australia, the UK and Europe lose money in two directions: politeness that reads as unreliability, and a client's blunt reply that reads as anger when it is not. You start by learning what a client is actually reading for, which is whether they can predict you and whether they have to chase you. Then you build the routine messages that make a client relax: the standing update, the question that gets one clear answer, the recap that turns a verbal instruction into a written record. Then the hard ones: refusing extra work by naming what it changes, sending a delay message the day you know rather than the day it lands, and talking about money without shrinking. The last chapter covers repair and renewal: answering an unhappy client, owning a mistake in one sentence instead of five paragraphs, and the messages that bring the next project. Every lesson is written for a Filipino freelancer with foreign clients. You finish with a set of message shapes you can reuse across clients and trades.
skills: Money and rate conversations in writing
outcomes: Send a weekly update in a fixed shape so a client never has to ask where things are
Refuse or renegotiate extra work by naming what it changes, instead of absorbing it silently
Send bad news the day you learn it, with the fix and the decision the client has to make
Ask one question that gets one answer, instead of a wall of questions that gets none
Answer an unhappy client without grovelling and without going quiet, and keep the relationship
roles: Virtual assistants and freelancers with foreign clients
Remote jobseekers applying to overseas roles
Customer support and BPO staff moving into freelance work
Anyone whose client work lives in email, Slack and chat

lessons.title: What competence sounds like in writing
lessons.content_mdx:
# What competence sounds like in writing

Two messages reach the same client on the same Tuesday morning.

Ramon writes: "Hi Sir, sorry to disturb. I hope you are doing well. I just wanted to ask kindly if maybe the deadline for the report could possibly be moved a little, if that is okay with you? Sorry again for the trouble. Thank you so much po."

Bea writes: "Hi Dan, the report needs one more day. I can send it Thursday morning your time instead of Wednesday. Nothing else in the project moves. If Wednesday is hard for you, say so and I will drop the competitor section to make it."

Same request. Same courtesy underneath. Roughly the same English. One of those two people is easier to work with, and it is not the one who apologised twice.

## What a client is reading for

When your message arrives, a client is answering three questions, whether or not they could name them.

**Can I predict this person?** Do things arrive when they said, in the shape they said, or do I find out at the end?

**Will I have to chase them?** If I go quiet for a week, will I still know where this project is?

**Did they answer what I asked?** I sent one question. Is the answer in here, and can I find it without reading twice?

Notice what is not on that list. Vocabulary is not on it. Grammar is not on it. A sentence like "I will send it Thursday morning" survives a missing article and still does its job. A flawless paragraph that never names a day does not do its job at all, however correct it is.

That is the argument this whole course rests on. It assumes your English already works well enough to do the job. What it fixes is register and structure, and both are fixable in the next message you send.

## The apologetic register

Here is what it looks like in the wild. Read your own sent folder afterwards and see how much of it you recognise.

- Opening with an apology instead of information: "Sorry for the trouble" before the client knows what the trouble is.
- Asking permission to speak: "I just wanted to ask if maybe it would be possible to..."
- Hedging until the sentence evaporates: "possibly", "a little", "if that is okay", "I will try my best".
- Promising effort instead of a date. "I will do my best to finish soon" gives a client nothing to plan around.
- Apologising for a reply that was not late.

Each of those does something you did not intend. A reader who has to hunt through three sentences to find the actual request has been handed work, not information. And a message that opens braced for failure invites the reader to start looking for the failure.

None of this is about being humble. Humility is fine. The problem is that on a page, shrinking and uncertainty look identical.

## The four swaps

**Replace apology with information.** Instead of "So sorry for the delay in my reply", write "Here is where the tracker stands." If you genuinely were late and it mattered, one sentence covers it: "Apologies for the slow reply, I was on the migration all day. Here is where it landed."

**Replace hedging with a date or a number you can keep.** Not "I will try to have it soon" but "Thursday, end of my day." Not "it might take a while" but "two working days once I have the logins." That rule has teeth in the other direction too: never name a date you are not willing to be held to.

**Anchor every date to their clock, not yours.** End of day is a different Tuesday in Manila and in Melbourne, and the one your client will hold you to is the one on their calendar. Write Thursday morning your time, or before you start on Thursday. It costs three words, and it takes away a whole class of deadlines that were met in Manila and missed in Melbourne.

**Replace "I hope this is okay" with "here is what I did and why."** Aileen, a VA in Davao, used to send drafts with "I hope this is what you wanted, sorry if not." She now sends: "I went with the shorter headline because the long one broke on mobile. Say the word and I will switch it back." Same draft, same person. She stopped asking to be forgiven for working.

## Warmth is not what you are cutting

There is a bad version of this lesson where you read it and turn cold. Do not.

Greeting people by name stays. Thanking someone who actually did something stays. Noticing that a client mentioned a sick parent stays. Filipino courtesy is not a liability, and no client is asking you to become a robot.

What goes is the shrinking: the pre-emptive sorry, the permission-asking, the hedge wrapped around a commitment you were about to make anyway. Warm and clear is a real combination, and it is the one you are aiming at.

## Before the next lesson

Open your sent messages and read the last five you wrote to a client. Count the apologies. Circle every sentence that promises effort instead of a date. Then rewrite one of those messages: keep the greeting, cut the shrinking, and put the answer in the first line.

lessons.title: Tone that gets misread in both directions
lessons.content_mdx:
# Tone that gets misread in both directions

Kaye, a VA in Iloilo, spent a Sunday night convinced she was about to be fired. Her client in Melbourne had answered a long, careful message with one word: "Fine." She reread it until midnight. On Monday he sent her a new project.

That same client had been telling a friend he could never get a straight answer out of Kaye about whether she could take on more hours.

Two misreadings, one working relationship, and both people thought they were being perfectly polite.

## Direction one: courtesy that arrives as evasion

Filipino professional politeness protects the other person from an awkward moment. That instinct is worth keeping. What it does inside a business message in English is quietly remove the information.

**The refusal that never refuses.** "I will try." "Let me see." "Maybe next week." "I will check my schedule." In a Philippine office these are understood. To a client who takes words at face value, they are a soft yes, and he plans around them. When the thing does not arrive, he does not think she was being polite. He thinks she said she would.

If the answer is no, use the word no. "I cannot take that on this week. I can start it Monday." That is not rude. It is the most useful thing you can hand a person who is trying to plan.

**Silence where a no belongs.** Not replying at all to a request you cannot meet is the strongest version of the same problem. Silence is never read as a refusal. It is read as an unknown, and unknowns are what make a client anxious.

**Fossilised business English.** "Kindly revert." "For your kind consideration." "Please be informed." "Please be guided accordingly." Nobody should feel bad for using the English they were taught, and none of these is an error. But they belong to a formal letter tradition, and a client typing to you from a phone between meetings is not writing in that tradition. The gap makes you sound like a form instead of a person. "Let me know" does everything "kindly revert" does, and sounds like someone he can talk to.

**Po and opo carried into English.** With a Filipino client they cost nothing. With a client who does not speak Tagalog, the word cannot land, because he has no idea what work it is doing. Respect then has to be carried by things he can read: his name, a clear answer, and work that arrives.

**A smiley doing a sentence's job.** A smiley softening "the deadline moved" is being asked to carry a concession, an apology and a reassurance all at once. Write the sentence instead.

**Apology inflation.** Sorry for the delay, sorry for the trouble, sorry for the many questions, sorry again. One of those is nothing. Four in one message change what the message is about: it stops being about the work and becomes about your discomfort, which the client now has to manage on top of his own week.

## Direction two: bluntness that is not anger

Now the other side, and this is the one that costs Filipino freelancers sleep.

A client writes "No, do it this way." Or "Fine." Or a reply with no greeting, no thanks and no sign-off, from the same person who wrote three warm paragraphs last week.

Before you build a story out of it, run one test. Read it again and ask: is there a criticism of me in here, or only an instruction about the work? "No, do it this way" carries no criticism. It carries a decision.

People compress when they are busy, and the softeners go first, because they are the part carrying the least information. A one-word reply can simply mean the person was walking into a meeting. That is a fact about their afternoon, not a verdict on you.

What you do next matters more than what you felt. Reply at the size the message deserves. Answer a five-word instruction with three paragraphs of apology and you have turned a two-second correction into an event, and now your client has a situation to handle that he did not have before.

## Long writers and fragment writers

Some clients write essays. Some send six fragments in a row and expect the same back. Match the length and the speed, because that is what makes you easy to read. Do not match the slang, the sarcasm or the swearing. Borrowed informality lands badly when it is not yours.

## The only safe way to hold any of this

Somewhere you will read that Americans are direct, that Germans are blunt, that the British never say what they mean. Treat every one of those sentences as a hypothesis about the single person you are working with, never as a fact about a country. Your client is one individual with a job, a mood and a writing habit, and the evidence for how she communicates is already sitting in your inbox.

So read the evidence. How long are her messages? Does she greet you? Does she answer at night? Then ask her outright in the first week: "How do you want to hear from me, and what would you rather I just decide on my own?" That one question replaces every article you will ever read about her nationality.

## Before the next lesson

Find the last client message that unsettled you. Underline only the parts that are about the work. Then write the reply you would have sent if you had read nothing but the underlined parts.

lessons.title: The shape of a message that gets read
lessons.content_mdx:
# The shape of a message that gets read

Miguel, a developer in Cagayan de Oro, sent his client a message on a Wednesday afternoon. Four hundred words: what he had tried, why the first approach failed, what he read, what he decided, what he still needed. Real work, honestly reported.

The client replied: "so is it done?"

The information was all in there. It was in paragraph three.

## Answer first, reasons after

Put the answer, the decision or the ask in the first line. Everything that explains it goes underneath.

This feels backwards if you were taught to build toward a conclusion. In a client message the conclusion goes on top, because your reader may get one line before something interrupts her, and the person who reads only that line should still walk away correctly informed.

Before: "I looked into the plugin conflict and tried three different versions, and after going through the logs I found the caching layer was the real issue, so the site will be ready tomorrow."

After: "The site will be ready tomorrow. It was a caching conflict, not the plugin. Detail below if you want it."

Same facts. In the second one the client can stop after eight words and still know the thing she needed to know.

## One message, one job

A message that does three jobs gets one reply, and you do not get to choose which one.

So split by job. A decision the client has to make goes in its own message, because it needs a reply and you want to be able to see whether it got one. Things she only needs to know can travel together. Four small questions can share a message. A decision and a progress report should not, because the progress report gives her somewhere comfortable to stop reading.

## The subject line names the decision, not the topic

"Website" is a topic. So is "Update". So is "Quick question".

A subject line here has one job: tell a person scanning an inbox what will be required of them, and by when. "Need your pick between two homepage photos by Friday." "Invoice attached, no action needed." "Blocked on the API key, cannot continue Monday without it."

This is not about writing a subject line that earns an open from a stranger. That is marketing copy and it belongs to a different course. This is about someone who already works with you being able to sort you in two seconds.

## Make it survive a phone screen

Assume the first read happens on a phone, walking.

Short paragraphs, one idea each, with a blank line between them. Options as a list, each one labelled so it can be pointed at: "Option A: keep the original photo, no extra cost, ready Friday." Bold once in a message or not at all, because bolding four things bolds nothing.

Never a wall of text. Never a telegram either: a message so clipped that the client has to write back asking what you mean has cost you a round trip and a day.

## What goes in writing, and what does not

In writing: anything carrying a date, a number, a scope or a commitment. If being misremembered on it would hurt, it is written.

On a call or in a short screen recording: something visual that would take four paragraphs to describe, or a disagreement that two written rounds have not moved. Text is good at record and bad at tone under pressure.

And the rule that joins them: anything decided out loud gets written down afterwards, by you, the same day. You will build that recap properly in the next chapter. For now hold the habit only: a call is not finished until a message summarising it exists.

One message this course does not cover: the first one you send to a stranger who has not hired you yet. A reply to a job post, a cold email, a follow-up after a discovery call. That is a different craft with a different reader, and it belongs to Freelancing Fundamentals. Everything here assumes somebody has already said yes.

## When the message is not an email

A good part of your client writing lands in a chat window instead: Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, the message box inside a platform. Everything above still holds. What changes is how it gets read.

A chat client answers in fragments. You send four things and get back "ok", then six minutes later, "wait which one". The answer is not to write less. It is to make each part separable.

So put one idea per message, and send them as separate messages rather than as one block with line breaks inside it. Then the client can answer the part they have an answer for and come back to the rest, instead of parking all of it until they have time for the whole thing. Number them when there is more than one: "1 of 3" tells someone scanning on a phone how much is coming.

Put a decision in its own message, on its own line, with nothing after it. A question at the bottom of a long fragment is the one that gets missed, and then you have waited a day for an answer nobody knew you needed.

And when a chat thread settles something with a date, a number or a scope in it, move it. Paste the agreed line into email or the shared doc the same day, so it sits somewhere that does not scroll. A month later nobody can find what was agreed in chat, and the person who loses that argument is the one who did the work.

## Before the next lesson

Take the longest message you sent a client this month and rewrite it as one first line plus three short paragraphs. Then check it: if she read only the first line and nothing else, would she have the answer?

quiz.prompt: Paolo has been building a client's landing page for four days and has sent nothing in that time. On Thursday his client Nathan messages: "Hey, where are we on the landing page?" Which opening line should Paolo's reply start with?

options.text: The landing page goes to you Monday morning. Two sections are finished and the pricing block is being built now.
Sorry for the silence since Monday. I know you have been waiting and I should have sent you something days ago.
Hi Nathan, hope the week is going well over there. Sending a quick update on the landing page ahead of Friday.
I am working as fast as I can on the landing page and I will have it over to you as soon as it is ready.

quiz.explanation: Nathan asked one question: where are we. The answer is a date and a status, and it belongs in the first line where he will actually meet it. Option b opens with an apology before Nathan has been told anything, so he reads a whole sentence to discover he still does not know. Option c spends the opening on pleasantries and then only promises an update rather than giving one. Option d is the effort promise: as soon as it is ready is not a date, and a client cannot plan around it. Paolo can still be warm, and should be, but courtesy goes after the answer, not in front of it.

quiz.prompt: Grace sends two design options with a short recommendation. Her client, who has written her long friendly messages for a month, replies in full: "No. Option B. Move on." There is no greeting and nothing else. What should Grace do?

options.text: Ask him whether something is wrong, since this reply is much colder than every other message he has sent her.
Apologise for pushing the wrong option, explain her reasoning in full, and promise to be more careful next time.
Build option B, reply in one line saying it is under way and when it will land, then carry on with her week.
Leave it overnight so he can cool down first, then send a warmer message the next morning to reset things.

quiz.explanation: Read the message for what it contains rather than what it lacks. There is no criticism of Grace in it. There is a decision and an instruction, from someone who was probably typing while walking. The right size of reply matches the size of the message. Option a hands him an emotional errand he did not ask for. Option b turns a two-second correction into an incident and invites him to manage her feelings. Option d is worse than it looks: going quiet for a day after a client makes a decision is the thing that actually creates a problem, because now he does not know whether the work has started.

quiz.prompt: Joel has to tell a client that this month's report will use last quarter's figures, because the current quarter is not closed. He has drafted four paragraphs: how the reporting cycle works, the risk of using older figures, his decision to use last quarter and label it clearly, and a thank you. What should he do before sending?

options.text: Send it as it stands, because the client needs the background first or the decision will not make sense to him.
Move the decision up to the first line and keep all of the background below it for the client who wants it.
Cut it down to the decision on its own, since background is what makes a client stop reading a message.
Ask for a call instead, because a judgement call about which figures to use is too involved for a message.

quiz.explanation: Answer first, reasons after. A client who reads one line gets the decision; a client with two minutes scrolls down and gets the reasoning. Nothing is lost by reordering and a great deal is lost by burying. Option a assumes the client will read as far as paragraph three, which is the assumption that got Joel here. Option c overcorrects into a telegram and costs a round trip when the client writes back asking why. Option d moves a written, checkable decision into a call where it leaves no record, and it is exactly the sort of thing that has to be written down afterwards anyway.

quiz.prompt: Errol sends his client one message containing a progress note, a question about which pricing tier to feature, and a request for the brand font files. The client replies only about the fonts. This is the third time it has happened. What is the fix?

options.text: Send the very same message again the next morning, since a client who answers part of it has only skimmed it.
Keep the three items in one message but number them, so the client can see there are three things to answer.
Put the pricing question at the top of the message and bold it, so it is the first thing he sees on opening.
Send the decision he needs as its own message, and keep the progress note and the file request separate.

quiz.explanation: A message doing three jobs gets one reply, and the client chooses which job, usually the easiest one. One message, one job: a decision travels alone so that a missing reply is visible instead of hidden inside a thread that technically got answered. Option a repeats the same structure and gets the same result. Option b makes the three items countable and changes nothing else, because the progress note is still sitting there as a comfortable place to stop reading. Option c helps for one message and stops helping the moment you bold two things.

quiz.prompt: Vince works with a client who runs everything through chat and answers in fragments. He has a progress note to give, a blocked item to flag, and one decision he needs on the banner size. How should he send it?

options.text: Three separate messages, with the decision on its own and nothing after it, numbered so he sees what is coming.
One message with all three things in it, split by line breaks, so the whole picture arrives in a single place.
One message with the decision at the bottom, after the progress note, so the client has the context first.
The progress note now, and the blocked item and the decision tomorrow, so he is not filling up the chat window.

quiz.explanation: A client in a chat window answers the part they have an answer for and leaves the rest, so make each part separable and let them do exactly that. The decision travels on its own with nothing after it, because a question at the bottom of a long fragment is the one that gets missed. Option b arrives as one block and gets one reply, which is the same failure the line breaks were meant to solve. Option c buries the decision under the news. Option d holds a decision back for a day for a tidiness nobody asked for, and the blocked item ages while it waits.

quiz.prompt: Rico's monthly package covers blog posts and the newsletter. His client messages: "Does the package include the Instagram graphics, or is that separate?" Which reply is best?

options.text: Thanks for asking! Let me go over my notes on what we agreed and I will come back to you on this shortly.
Separate. The package covers the blog posts and the newsletter, so the graphics would be their own piece.
The package was built around a monthly writing load, and graphics sit outside that, so they are separate.
I would be very happy to include them if it helps you, I really do not want this to become a problem for us.

quiz.explanation: The client asked a yes or no question about scope and deserves the yes or no in the first word, followed by what the package does cover so the boundary is visible instead of implied. Option c carries exactly the same fact as option b and is still the weaker message, because the answer arrives at the end, after a clause about how the package was built. A client reading on a phone meets the reasoning first and the answer last. Option a delays a fact Rico already knows, which reads as disorganised or as buying time to work out how to say no. Option d gives the work away to avoid a moment of friction, and does it so apologetically that the client learns the scope moves whenever he asks.

quiz.prompt: Before her first message to a new client in Berlin, Trisha reads a blog post saying German clients are blunt and dislike small talk, so she drafts a message with no greeting and no sign-off. The client's own messages so far have been long, warm and full of questions. What has gone wrong?

options.text: Nothing yet. Matching the writing conventions of a client's country is the safest opening move you can make.
She should keep the blunt style but add a greeting, since a greeting is expected in business email everywhere.
She should write in her own natural style and ignore how he writes, because copying anyone always reads as fake.
She swapped a claim about a whole country for the evidence in front of her, which is how this client actually writes.

quiz.explanation: Any sentence that begins with a nationality is a hypothesis about one person at best, and Trisha has an inbox full of direct evidence about how this particular person writes. Match the individual, not the article. Option a treats a generalisation as a rule and has her write coldly to someone who writes warmly. Option b patches the surface while keeping the same broken method underneath. Option c overshoots the other way: matching a client's length and pace is not imitation, it is making yourself easy for that person to read, and it stops well short of borrowing their slang.

quiz.prompt: Nika needs her client to choose between two homepage photos by Friday, or the launch slips to the following week. She is sending an email. Which subject line does the job?

options.text: Homepage update, plus a few other things from this week
Quick question whenever you have a moment, no rush at all
Need your pick between two homepage photos, Friday deadline
URGENT: homepage photos, please respond immediately

quiz.explanation: A subject line written to someone who already works with you should say what is required and by when, so it can be sorted in two seconds from a phone. Option c does both. Option a names a topic and buries the decision behind other things. Option b actively tells the client it can wait, which is the opposite of true and is the sentence Nika will regret on Friday. Option d shouts without saying what is needed, and an urgency marker stops working the second time you use one, so keep it for something that cannot be described.

lessons.title: The standing update
lessons.content_mdx:
# The standing update

Marilou does admin support from Naga for a client in Melbourne. Her first month went well. She cleared every task, fixed two things nobody asked her to fix, and said almost nothing. On the last Friday the client wrote: "Just checking, everything okay on your end?"

Nothing was wrong. She had simply been quiet, and he had spent a week filling the silence himself.

That is the whole problem. A client who cannot see you cannot tell the difference between a freelancer who is busy and one who has gone. Silence is never read as everything is fine. It reads as unknown, and unknown is the state a client hires someone to remove.

## Fixed day, fixed shape, sent first

One habit fixes it. A short update, on the same day every week, in the same shape, sent before anyone asks.

Four headings do the work.

- **Done.** What is finished, and where they can see it.
- **In progress.** What you are on now, and the day it lands.
- **Waiting on.** What is blocked, and whose desk it is sitting on. Name the person.
- **Next.** What you pick up when the current thing is finished.

On a week where something went wrong, one line goes between Done and In progress: what happened. It is part of the shape, not an addition to it.

The shape matters more than the wording. A client who gets the same headings every week stops reading for reassurance and starts reading for changes. You become predictable, and predictable is the product.

## The week that went badly

Dennis builds websites from Baguio. One week his main project moved nowhere: two days lost to a family emergency, and the product photos he had asked for never arrived. His instinct was to skip the update and send a bigger one next week, once he had something to show.

Skipping is exactly the wrong move. The update on a bad week is the one that buys you trust, because it is the only one that costs you something to send.

What he sent:

> Update, week of the 14th.
> **Done:** nothing shipped this week.
> **What happened:** I lost two days to a family emergency, and the product photos I asked for on the 9th have not arrived, so the gallery is still blocked.
> **In progress:** back on the gallery today. It can be finished Thursday if the photos land by Tuesday.
> **Waiting on:** the photos, with you since the 9th.
> **Next:** pricing page.

No apology tour. No excuse buried in paragraph four. What happened, what it changed, what he needs. His client finished that message knowing more than he did before it, and knowing that part of the delay was his own.

## What an update is not

- **Not a diary of your hours.** "Spent three hours on research" tells a client nothing about whether anything is finished. Report status, not effort.
- **Not an essay.** If it does not survive on a phone screen, cut it. Two screens of scrolling is a document, not a status report.
- **Not a place to bury bad news.** A slipped date does not go in the middle of a cheerful list. Sending that one on its own is the next chapter's work.
- **Not a task list with no status.** "Gallery, pricing page, contact form" is a list. "Gallery done, pricing page Thursday, contact form blocked on your copy" is an update.

## Set the rhythm in week one

Do not perform the update. Agree it. In your first week, say it plainly:

> I send a written update every Friday morning, four lines, no call needed. Does Friday work, or is Monday more useful to you?

Two things happen. The update becomes something the client expects rather than something you are doing to prove yourself. And you find out how this particular client wants to be kept informed instead of guessing, which is the only reliable way to know it.

Then keep the day even on quiet weeks. A one-line update costs you a minute and keeps the habit alive for the week you actually need it.

## Where the lines come from

This course teaches the message. The system that makes those four lines true on the day you write them, a board you keep current across several clients, is project operations work and belongs to another course. If you run one or two clients, a running note on your phone that you add to as you finish things is enough.

The rule is only this: never assemble Friday's update from memory on Friday morning. You will forget the blocked item, which is the one line the client needed.

## Do this now

Write your next update in the four headings before Friday arrives. Send it whether or not the week went well.

lessons.title: A question that gets an answer
lessons.content_mdx:
# A question that gets an answer

Joy, a VA in Cavite, sent her London client this on a Tuesday afternoon:

> Hi! Quick questions po. Do you want the newsletter to go out Thursday or Friday? Also should I use the new logo or the old one? And do you have the discount code yet? For the header image, do you prefer the beach photo or the office one, or should I look for something else? Also let me know your thoughts on the subject line. Thank you!

Four days, no reply. The client was not ignoring her. He opened it on his phone, saw a pile of decisions, decided it needed a proper sit-down, and got on with his day.

## Why questions go unanswered

Three reasons, and all three belong to the sender.

**It arrives as a wall.** Five questions in one message is not five times more likely to be answered. It is one task that now looks large.

**It asks the client to do your thinking.** "What do you want the header image to be?" hands the whole problem back. "Which of these two?" hands over a decision.

**It carries no date.** A question with no deadline attached can be answered any time, which in practice means later.

## The build

One message, one decision. Then four parts.

1. **The decision, in the first line.** Name it. "One decision needed on the newsletter send date."
2. **Only the context that changes the answer.** Not the history. The two or three facts that matter.
3. **Options, with your recommendation.** Two or three, each with its consequence attached, and say which one you would pick and why. You are the specialist. Recommending is the job, not overstepping.
4. **A default and a date.** What you will do if you hear nothing, and by when.

That last part is what makes the message easy to leave alone. You have removed the risk of not replying, so a reply stops being an obligation and becomes a correction, which is a far smaller thing to sit down and do.

Joy's message, rebuilt:

> Newsletter send date, one decision. Thursday reaches people before the weekend. Friday clashes with your webinar invite going out the same morning, so I would go Thursday. If I have not heard from you by Wednesday 5pm your time, I will schedule it for Thursday and confirm once it is queued.

The other four questions get batched into a separate message, or she answers them herself.

## Batch, and do not drip

Do not send a client four separate questions across one afternoon. Collect the small ones, send them once, number them, and write each so it can be answered in a word.

And answer what you can yourself. If the brand colours are in the folder they handed you, do not ask what the brand colours are. A client who has to look things up on your behalf is doing your job. Where you had to make a call, say so in the update: "I used the blue from the logo file. Tell me if there is a newer brand sheet."

## Asking for access without three rounds

Requests for logins, files and permissions turn into a week of back and forth because they arrive vague. Ask in one shot:

> I need read access to the analytics account for the main site, sent to this email address. It is for the traffic section of the monthly report. Once you add me I will confirm I can see it, and I will not need anything else from you on this.

Name the exact thing, the exact account it should go to, what it is for, and what happens once you have it. If a client keeps offering to send you a password instead, ask to be added as a user, which is safer for both of you.

## Chasing without nagging

A question that has gone quiet gets one short chase, and the chase repeats the decision rather than the complaint:

> Following up on the send date. Still fine to go Thursday unless you tell me otherwise by 5pm.

No "just checking in", no "sorry to bother you", and nothing about how long you have been waiting. That last one reads as a grievance and gets you a defensive reply instead of an answer.

If it stalls again and the date is close, change the channel. A chat message when the email died, or a call request naming the single decision. Moving channels is not escalation, it is a different door.

And every standing update ends by restating whatever is still sitting with the client. A question they never answered should never quietly vanish from the record.

## Do this now

Take the last question you sent a client. Rewrite it as one decision, two options, your recommendation, and a date you will proceed without them.

lessons.title: Confirming what you heard
lessons.content_mdx:
# Confirming what you heard

Ronnie takes a call with a California client at ten at night, Manila time. The client talks fast for twenty minutes, changes direction twice, and finishes with "cool, so you'll get that over to me next week?" Ronnie says "Noted, will do."

Nine days later the client asks where the second version is. Ronnie did not know there was a second version.

## Noted is the most expensive word you use

"Noted." "Sure thing." "Copy." "Okay po." A thumbs up. All of them say the same thing, which is that sound arrived. None of them says what you understood. They feel efficient, and they quietly move the entire risk of a misunderstanding onto you, because the client now believes you agreed to whatever was in his head.

Replace it with a recap. After any call, voice note, or fast instruction in chat, send back what you took away, in writing, the same day.

## The shape

> From our call just now, here is what I have.
> **What I understood:** the landing page copy gets rewritten for the new offer, and you want a second, shorter headline version to test against it.
> **What I will do:** both versions in the shared doc by Wednesday.
> **What I need from you:** the new pricing. If it does not arrive by Tuesday I will use the figures on the current page.
> Tell me by tomorrow morning if I have any of this wrong.

Four minutes of typing. It is what stops the argument you would otherwise be having three weeks from now.

The invitation to correct is not weakness. It gives the client a cheap way to fix a small error today instead of an expensive one later, and it makes the record shared rather than something you imposed on them.

## Saying you did not understand

You will not catch everything, especially on a bad line with a fast talker, and pretending otherwise is how the wrong thing gets built. There is nothing embarrassing about this:

> I did not catch the part about the reporting. Could you put that one in writing so I get it exactly right?

Notice what it does not do. It does not apologise, it does not blame your English, and it does not blame the client's audio. It names the piece and asks for it in the format you need. Retyping one instruction costs a client far less than a wrong deliverable does, and asking is a reasonable thing to do.

If a client habitually gives instructions in voice notes, ask once: "Voice notes are fine for context. For anything with a date or a number in it, could you send a line of text too?"

## When you understood it and disagree

Confirm first, object once, then let them decide.

> Understood, we lead with the discount on the homepage. One flag before I build it: that block is where the free trial button currently sits, so the trial link moves below the fold. I am happy either way. Which do you want?

You have recorded the instruction, named the consequence in one sentence, and handed the decision back. You are not arguing, and you are not silently building something you believe is wrong. If they hold their position, build it. Your recap already shows you raised it.

## When they change their mind

They will, and sometimes they will remember the old instruction as something they never gave. This is the exact situation the recap exists for, and how you use it decides whether the relationship survives it.

Do not produce it like a receipt. Never write "as per my email of the 3rd." Write:

> No problem, I can switch to the short headline. So we are on the same page: my note from the 3rd had the long version as the one to build, which is what is in the doc now. Redoing it moves delivery to Friday instead of Wednesday.

Same facts, no accusation, and the cost stated instead of swallowed. Where the change is bigger than a redo, the next chapter has the wording for what it changes.

One boundary. These records are a working habit, not a legal instrument. Their value is that two people end the week remembering the same week. Nothing here is advice about contracts, and nothing here is a claim about what any message would do in a dispute.

## Do this now

After your next call or voice note, send the four-part recap the same day, and close it with the day by which a correction has to reach you.

quiz.prompt: Neneng keeps the books for a cafe group from Antipolo. This week she recorded nothing new: three days went to a family emergency, and the receipts she asked for at the start of the month have still not arrived. Her weekly update is due Friday morning. What should she send?

options.text: The usual Friday update, saying nothing was posted, why, what she still needs, and when the ledger catches up.
Nothing this Friday, then a fuller update next week once there is finished work she can actually show him.
A message apologising for the lost days and offering to work the weekend at no charge to make the time back.
The usual update with the ledger and the March reconciliation listed as in progress, and the lost days left out.

quiz.explanation: The update on a bad week is the one that buys trust, because it is the only one that costs something to send. Skipping it leaves the client to imagine the reason, and silence is never read as everything is fine. A long apology puts the attention on Neneng instead of on the receipts she needs, and free weekend work turns a shared delay into her debt. The last option is the one that ends relationships: the client finds out on the due date.

quiz.prompt: Joy has to schedule a newsletter today and needs one decision from her London client. She also has three smaller questions that can wait until next week. What goes in the message she sends now?

options.text: All four questions in one numbered list, so the client can work through them in a single sitting.
The send date, plus a note that three more questions are coming later once he has replied to this first one.
The send date only, with two options, her recommendation, and what she does if nothing lands by five today.
A request for a short call, since four open items are faster to settle out loud than in a long written thread.

quiz.explanation: One message, one decision, with a default attached. The default is what makes it easy to leave alone, and it has to fall before the moment she is forced to act. Batching is right for small questions, but not when one of them is urgent and the other three drag it into a sit-down job. Announcing that more questions are coming adds weight without adding information. A call to settle a two-option decision costs the client more time than the decision is worth, and leaves nothing in writing.

quiz.prompt: Ronnie ends a late call with his US client, who talked for half an hour and changed direction twice. Ronnie is clear on the main deliverable and lost one part about how the reporting should work. What does he do next?

options.text: Reply with a thumbs up tonight, start the work tomorrow, and ask about the reporting when he reaches it.
Wait for a written brief, since the client called the meeting and set the direction the work should take.
Listen back to his own recording of the call in the morning and rebuild the brief from it before replying.
Send a recap tonight: what he understood, what he will do, what he needs, and when to correct him.

quiz.explanation: The recap is the cheapest insurance in freelancing, and the same-day version is the one that works, because the client can still remember what he said. A thumbs up records only that sound arrived, and moves the whole risk of a misunderstanding onto Ronnie. Waiting for a brief that may never come burns the week. The recording helps him write the recap but is not a substitute for it: the point is that the client sees and confirms the version Ronnie is building from.

quiz.prompt: Riza runs email support for a Melbourne client and needs one decision from him to unblock a deliverable due Friday. She emailed the question on Monday. It is Wednesday, there is no reply, and no safe default exists on this one.

options.text: Resend the same email on Thursday with the subject line changed, since the first one probably went unread.
Chase once in a different channel, restating the one decision and what Friday looks like if it lands today.
Send a longer email explaining what the delay is costing and that she has now been waiting since Monday.
Wait until Friday, deliver everything else, and note in the update that this item was blocked on his answer.

quiz.explanation: One short chase that repeats the decision, and a move to a channel where he actually reads things, because the email is evidently not reaching him. A new subject line on the same email in the same inbox is the same message in the same place. Waiting until Friday is technically defensible and commercially terrible: the client learns on the due date that his own silence broke the date. The grievance email invites a defensive reply instead of a decision.

quiz.prompt: Aldrin needs access to a client's analytics to build the monthly report. His last two access requests each turned into a week of back and forth. Which message ends it in one round?

options.text: Ask whether the client would rather add him directly or have Aldrin walk him through the steps on a call.
Ask the client to send over the analytics login details whenever he gets a spare moment in the coming week.
Name the exact account and access level, the email to send it to, what it is for, and when he needs it.
Ask for admin access to the analytics account, since admin removes any chance of a second request later.

quiz.explanation: Access requests stall because they arrive vague, so the client does not know what to click or where to send it. Naming the account, the level, the destination address and the deadline leaves one action. Asking for login details invites a shared password, which is worse for both of you than being added as a user. Offering the client a choice adds a decision he did not want. Asking for admin when read access would do enlarges the request and gives him a reason to think about it, which is how it ends up parked.

quiz.prompt: On a call about the new brochure, Perla's client says in passing, "and while you're in there, can you sort out the email signatures for the team too?" Perla does not respond to it on the call. What goes in her recap that evening?

options.text: The signatures as a separate item, not started, with a question about whether they join this month's work.
Nothing about the signatures. It was a passing remark, and writing it down makes it look bigger than it was.
The signatures added to what she will deliver this week, since she heard it clearly and did not object then.
A line saying the signatures fall outside scope and cannot be touched until a new agreement is signed by both.

quiz.explanation: The recap's job is to make an out-loud remark visible so it can be decided rather than assumed. Listing the signatures separately, unstarted, with one question attached, does that without refusing anything. Leaving them out means the two of you carry different versions of the week. Folding them into this week's deliverables is how work gets absorbed silently and how a date slips. The flat refusal answers a question nobody has asked yet, and the wording of that answer is the next chapter's subject.

quiz.prompt: Four freelancers send their Friday update to the same client. Which one leaves the client with nothing to chase and nothing to guess at?

options.text: "Made good progress on the site this week, mostly on the gallery, and I will keep you posted as things move."
"Gallery live. Pricing page Thursday. Contact form blocked on your copy. Next: blog template. Still need photos."
"This week: gallery page, pricing page, contact form. Next week: blog template, testimonials, footer links."
"All good on my end and nothing blocking me, so let me know if you need anything else before the weekend."

quiz.explanation: Every item carries a status, a date or an owner, and the one thing sitting with the client is named. That is an update. Good progress and keep you posted describe effort, not state, and leave the client to ask. A bare list of page names looks organised but says nothing about what is finished or what is stuck. All good with nothing blocking me is the most expensive of the four, because it closes the question and the client stops looking until something breaks.

quiz.prompt: Dexter's client says the thumbnail was always meant to use the product shot, and asks why the lifestyle photo is in the file. Dexter's recap from the 3rd, which the client never corrected, says the lifestyle photo. What does Dexter write?

options.text: Agree to switch and say nothing about the recap, since correcting a client on a small point is not worth it.
Quote the recap line back with its date and ask him to confirm he is changing what was agreed.
Explain in detail how the misunderstanding happened, so the same thing does not recur on the next round.
Agree to switch, note plainly what his recap said, and give the new date the redo pushes delivery to.

quiz.explanation: Say yes, put the record in the sentence without accusation, and state what it costs in time. That keeps the relationship and stops the same swap happening free every week. Staying quiet feels gracious and teaches the client that changes are free and instant, which is how a week disappears. Producing the recap as evidence and asking him to admit a change turns a small correction into a dispute. A detailed post-mortem on a headline is more words than the problem deserves.
