modules.description: The messages that are hardest to send: the extra request that was never agreed, the delay you can see coming, and the price conversation. Wording only. What the work is worth is decided elsewhere.

lessons.title: The extra request that was never agreed
lessons.content_mdx:
# The extra request that was never agreed

Jhoanna runs the inbox and calendar for a client in the UK. On a Thursday afternoon a message lands: "While you're in there, can you also clean up the contact list? Shouldn't take long."

Nothing about that message is hostile. The client is not testing her. He genuinely does not know that cleaning up the contact list is two days of work, because he has never done it. That is scope creep in its ordinary form. It is a person who cannot see the size of the thing they just asked for.

## How it actually arrives

Almost never as a formal request. It arrives as a screenshot with no words. As one small thing. As a quick favour. As a question in a call that has become a task by the end of the sentence. Sometimes it arrives wrapped in praise: "You did such a good job on the deck, could you also do the one for Tuesday?"

The tell is not the tone. The tell is that you are being asked for something that was not in what you agreed to do.

## Two bad moves

**The flat no.** "That is outside our scope." True, cheap, and it makes a client feel told off for asking what seemed like a reasonable question. A client rarely knows where the edge of the scope sits, and it is not their job to.

**The silent yes.** You absorb it, then the next one. Nothing is said, so nothing is visible, and by the third month you are doing noticeably more work for the same money and resenting somebody who has no idea. This is the worse of the two, because it punishes you as well.

## The third move: yes, and here is what it changes

Agree in principle, then name what it changes: in time, in cost, or in what gets dropped instead. You are not refusing. You are showing the client a price tag they could not see, then handing them the decision.

> Happy to do the contact list. It is about two days of work, so either it goes in after the September reports and pushes those back a week, or we treat it as a separate piece. Which would you prefer?

Three things are working there. It opens with yes. It states the size as a fact rather than a complaint. It ends with a choice that belongs to the client, so it cannot be read as a demand.

## Wording that accuses nobody

Keep every sentence about the work, never about the person's behaviour. "That was not in our agreement" points at them. "That sits outside what we scoped, so here is what adding it would mean" points at the work.

Shapes worth keeping:

- "Yes, and here is what it moves."
- "I can do that this week if the newsletter waits until next. Your call."
- "That is a different piece of work from the one we agreed. Want me to price it separately?"
- "Before I start: is this replacing the report, or in addition to it?"

And one to delete from your vocabulary: never write "no problem" about something that is a problem.

## Absorbing, out loud

Some requests really are small and you should just do them. Goodwill is real, and a five minute favour buys more than it costs.

Absorb it, then make it visible in one line in your next update. "Also fixed the two broken links on the About page, not billed, took ten minutes." That turns invisible free work into something the client can see, and establishes without any argument that these things have a size.

## When the pattern is the problem

A run of small requests is not several problems. It is one problem, and raising each one separately makes you look petty while nothing changes.

Raise the pattern once, in writing, as a proposal a reasonable person can say yes to.

> Over the last month there have been a run of small extras on top of the retainer. Each one is fine on its own, but together they are taking up the part of the week the reports used to have. Could we either add a fixed block of hours for ad hoc requests, or agree that anything over half an hour gets confirmed first?

That is a proposal, not a grievance. A client can answer it in one line.

## Where this lesson stops

This lesson owns the sentences. What the extra work is actually worth, and how to price it against the scope you agreed, belongs to Freelancing Fundamentals. Writing the change into the plan and working out which date moves belongs to Project and Client Operations. Your job here is narrower and it is enough: the client learns what their request costs before they confirm it.

## Before the next lesson

Find the last extra request you absorbed without saying so. Write the one line you would have added to your next update to make it visible, then use that line on the next one that arrives.

lessons.title: Bad news, early
lessons.content_mdx:
# Bad news, early

Marlon builds websites from Davao. On a Monday he opened the client's product file and found the data in a format his import would not read. Fixing it by hand was the better part of a week. The launch was Friday.

He said nothing. He told himself he could still make it, and he nearly did. On Thursday night he knew he could not, and he sent the message on Friday morning.

The delay was a few days. The damage was not the few days. It was that his client had spent the week telling her own team, and a partner, that Friday was happening.

## Timing beats wording

Rewrite that Friday message any way you like. Make it warm, make it professional, apologise beautifully. It still lands as a broken promise, because it arrived on the day the promise was due.

Send the same news on Monday and it is not a broken promise at all. It is a problem the two of you are managing together, with four working days in hand before anyone outside has to be told. Same delay. Completely different relationship.

So the rule is about the calendar, not about your English: **the day you can see the delay is the day you send the message.** Not the day you are certain. The day you can see it.

One boundary before the wording. Spotting the slip before it lands, from the signals in your own plan and your own record of timings, is Project and Client Operations' subject. This lesson starts at the moment you can see it, and it owns the message.

## The four parts

1. **What happened**, in one sentence. Not the investigation, the conclusion.
2. **What it means for their date.** A new date, or an honest "I will have a date for you by Wednesday."
3. **What you are already doing** about it.
4. **What you need them to decide**, if anything.

> The product file is in a format the import cannot read, so it has to be rebuilt by hand. That moves launch from Friday to the following Wednesday. I have started the rebuild and I am doing the payment pages in parallel so nothing else slips. If Friday is fixed for you, we can launch on Friday with the six main products only and add the rest the week after. Tell me which you would rather have and I will plan around it.

Nothing there is an apology and nothing is a defence. It is a status, a date, an action and a question.

## What not to do

- **Do not bury it.** A delay tucked into paragraph four of a cheerful update reads as concealment the moment the client notices.
- **Do not open with "just checking in".** You are not checking in. Say the thing in the first line.
- **Do not promise a recovery you cannot make.** "I will still hit Friday" bought Marlon four days and cost him the client's trust. A date you meet is worth more than a date they wanted.
- **Do not go quiet to think about it.** The hours you spend composing are hours the client could have spent deciding.

## Holding a date the client does not like

Sometimes the honest new date is worse than what they want to hear, and they push back. Hold it, without hardening.

> I understand the pressure on your side. Wednesday is the date I can actually meet. If Friday matters more than completeness, the version I can give you on Friday is the six main products with the rest following. Both are real options. What I cannot do is promise the full set on Friday.

You are not being difficult. You are refusing to sell them a second broken promise on the same project.

## The fear that keeps the message in drafts

The fear is that saying it early makes you look incompetent. Test that against what the client actually loses. It is not the days. It is the chance to react: to warn her own boss, to move a launch, to reorder her week. The surprise is the part that made her look bad, and the surprise is the part you control.

Early disclosure hands them time, options and a chance to look organised. Late disclosure hands them an ambush. The freelancer who says "this will slip, here is the plan" on Monday reads as someone watching their work closely. That is what competence looks like from outside.

## The smaller version: the estimate that was wrong

Not every piece of bad news is a missed deadline. Sometimes you said three days, and by the first afternoon you can see it is six.

Say so that afternoon, plainly, with the corrected number and one sentence of cause. "The sheet has far more duplicate rows than the sample showed, so this is closer to six days than three. Do you want the full clean, or the priority columns only inside the original three?"

A wrong estimate corrected on day one is a revision. The same correction on day three is a surprise, and on day four it is an excuse. The estimate was never the promise. Keeping the client's picture accurate is the promise.

## Do this now

Look at what you are working on now and name the earliest date you could have seen a slip coming. Write the four-part message for it today, even if you never send it.

lessons.title: Talking about money in English
lessons.content_mdx:
# Talking about money in English

Plainly, before anything else: this lesson does not help you decide what to charge. What your work is worth, and how to build a number from your own costs, are Freelancing Fundamentals' subject. This lesson is wording and timing only. The number is yours.

Money is where the shrinking is worst. The sentence gets longer, an apology appears at the front, and the number drifts to the end where it can be skimmed past. That reads as uncertainty about the number itself, and uncertainty opens a negotiation you never intended to open.

## Send a quote as a statement

A quote is information, not a request for permission. Number early, scope attached, then stop.

> Redesign of the six product pages: [your figure], invoiced in two parts, the first on start. Includes two rounds of changes. Does not include photography or the writing. I can start Monday if you confirm by Thursday.

The long paragraph explaining why you are worth it is the part that invites a haggle, because a case can be argued with. A number with a scope attached is just a fact. If they want the reasoning, they will ask.

## When they ask you to lower it

Two things can move: the price, or the work. Move the work.

> I can do that number for four pages with one round of changes. The full six page version stays at [your figure].

That keeps your rate intact and gives them a real choice. Discount the same scope and you have taught this client that your first number is decorative, so every future quote opens as a negotiation.

If you are simply holding: "That is my rate for this scope. I completely understand if the budget is not there this time." Then stop typing. The pause after is not rudeness, and filling it is how people talk themselves down.

## Turning down work that pays too little

Never insult the budget. The person with nothing this quarter may have a real budget next quarter, and they remember who was decent about it.

> Thanks for thinking of me. At that budget I would not be able to do the work properly, so I would rather not take it on than give you a thin version. If the budget changes later, send it over and I will make room.

Door open, no lecture, no counter-offer nobody asked for.

## Raising your rate with a client you already have

Deciding to raise it is a commercial decision, and how to arrive at the new number belongs to Freelancing Fundamentals. The message is three lines: notice, the new figure, the date it starts.

> From the January invoices my rate for this work goes to [your figure]. Everything else stays the same. Wanted to give you plenty of notice so it is not a surprise.

No apology. No essay about your costs. No offer to discuss it unless they raise it. Send it when nothing is on fire, never in the middle of a deadline and never attached to a complaint.

## Asking about a payment that has not arrived

The first ask is not a confrontation. Write it as though it were an oversight. If it is one, you have made it easy to fix. If it is not, you have lost nothing and the second ask is still there.

> Hi Ana, the March invoice was due last Friday and I do not think it has come through. Can you let me know when it is scheduled?

Named, dated, one question, no apology for asking. Never open with "sorry to bother you", and never write "no rush", because it is not true and the client will believe you.

The second ask, a week later, keeps the same manners and adds a consequence you will actually apply.

> Still nothing on the March invoice. I will hold the April work until it clears, which I would rather not do, so let me know if something is stuck on your side.

One condition on that last sentence. Write it only if pausing work is something you agreed at the start and are willing to actually do. A consequence you announce and then do not apply teaches the client that your dates are decoration, and a stoppage you never agreed to can put you in the wrong on your own terms, or on a platform's.

How far that ladder goes, whether you have the right to pause at all, and what happens after are decisions covered in Freelancing Fundamentals. What this lesson gives you is the sentence for each rung, which is the part that stalls people.

## Where a figure would help you

Sooner or later a real number matters: what a transfer costs you, what an exchange rate does to a quote, what you owe and when. Do not take those from a lesson, a forum post or a friend. Look them up at the source on the day you need them, from the provider's own page or the agency itself, and write down the date you checked.

Fees, rates and filing rules change. A confident wrong number in an email to a client is not a style problem. It is your money.

## Do this now

Take your last quote and cut everything that came before the number. Read what is left, and see whether anything you deleted was doing real work.

quiz.prompt: Bles handles the product listings for a homewares seller in Cebu on a monthly retainer. On a Thursday he asks her to also write FAQ copy for the whole catalogue, calling it quick. She estimates it at three full days. Which reply protects both the scope and the relationship?

options.text: "Happy to do this. It is three days of work, so either the listings move a week or we add it separately."
"This falls outside the scope we agreed at the start, so I cannot include it in this month's retainer."
"Sure, no problem at all, I will find a way to fit this in somewhere this week alongside the listings."
"Let me see what I can do with this one, and I will try my best to get to it before the end of the month."

quiz.explanation: Agree in principle, then name what it changes and hand the choice back. The client cannot see that the task is three days, so showing him the cost is information rather than a refusal. The flat no makes a reasonable question feel like a mistake. The silent yes buries three days of unpaid work where nobody will ever see it. Trying her best names no size, no date and no decision, so the request simply stays open.

quiz.prompt: On Monday, Grace opens a client's bank statements for the quarter and finds they are photo scans rather than exports, so every line has to be keyed in by hand. That puts Friday's management accounts out of reach. She thinks she might still recover some of it over the weekend. What should she do?

options.text: Keep going and send an update on Thursday, once she knows for certain whether Friday is achievable or not.
Add a line about the risk to Friday's regular update, kept light so the client is not alarmed too early.
Message him on Monday with what she found, the new date, and a choice between partial accounts and a later set.
Work through the weekend first, then tell him on Monday with the problem fixed and the date recovered.

quiz.explanation: The day you can see the delay is the day you send the message. On Monday the client still has time to warn his own people and to choose, so it stays a shared problem. By Thursday the same news is a broken promise, and inside Friday's update it reads as concealment. Fixing it silently over the weekend gambles his week on a recovery she cannot guarantee, and if it fails he finds out with no time left at all.

quiz.prompt: Emman quotes a gym in Pasig for a batch of twelve short videos. The client replies that he likes the work but has about two thirds of that to spend, and asks whether Emman can bring the number down. Which response holds the rate without ending the conversation?

options.text: Lower the figure to keep the client, and make up the difference by working faster through the later videos.
Offer eight videos with one round of changes at that budget, and keep the twelve at the figure he quoted.
Send a detailed breakdown of how the figure was reached, so the client can see the value he is getting for it.
Reply that the quoted price is final, and that he does not negotiate on rates once a quote has gone out.

quiz.explanation: Two things can move, the price or the work, and moving the work is what keeps your rate intact. The client gets a genuine choice instead of a wall. Discounting the same scope teaches him that the first number was decorative, so every future quote opens as a negotiation. A long justification is a case, and a case can be argued line by line. The flat refusal is defensible and socially expensive over a budget question anyone might ask.

quiz.prompt: Over a month, Lianne's retainer client has sent a steady drip of small extra tasks. Each one alone is minor. Together they have eaten the part of her week that the monthly reports used to occupy. How should she raise it?

options.text: Reply to the next small request by pointing out that this keeps happening and is becoming hard to sustain.
Keep absorbing them, while noting in each update that the task was extra, and wait for the client to notice.
Say nothing until renewal, then raise the retainer figure without explaining what the increase is actually for.
Send one message describing the pattern and proposing two ways to handle ad hoc requests from here on.

quiz.explanation: A run of small requests is one problem, not several, so raise it once and make it easy to agree to. Two workable options turn a grievance into a proposal a client can answer in a line. Attaching it to the next request makes one small task carry a month of accumulated feeling. Silent absorption plus hints leaves the client to solve a problem nobody has told him about. A raised figure with no reason attached looks arbitrary and invites the argument she was avoiding.

quiz.prompt: An inquiry arrives with a budget far below what the work would take. The company is well known in her industry and Kris would like to work with them eventually. What is the best reply?

options.text: Take it at their budget anyway, since a paying client now often leads to better paid work later on.
Send the full quote with no comment on the budget, and let them work out for themselves that it is short.
Explain that the budget is unrealistic for work of this kind and that they should reconsider what they set.
Say what she would need to do it properly, decline for now, and invite them back when the budget grows.

quiz.explanation: Decline the number, not the person, and leave the door visibly open. That is the version they remember next quarter, when the budget is real. Taking underpriced work sets the rate they will expect forever and fills the calendar a good client would have needed. A silent full quote reads as ignoring what they just told you. Telling a stranger their budget is unrealistic makes them feel corrected, which costs you the future conversation for nothing.

quiz.prompt: Lorna quoted two days to turn a client's workshop notes into a slide deck. On the first morning she finds the notes are photographs of a whiteboard rather than a document, and can see the job is closer to four days. What should she do about the estimate?

options.text: Work the two days, hand over the slides she has finished, and explain the rest during the handover call.
Tell the client that morning, with the revised estimate and a smaller option inside the original two days.
Absorb the extra days without saying anything about it, since she gave the estimate and should stand behind it.
Wait until the second day, when she can give the new estimate with a lot more confidence behind the number.

quiz.explanation: A wrong estimate corrected on the first morning is a revision. The same correction on the last day is a surprise, and after the deadline it sounds like an excuse. Offering a shorter deck inside the original two days gives the client a decision instead of a bill. Delivering half a job and explaining at handover moves the shock to the worst possible moment. Silently absorbing two days hides a change he would have wanted to weigh, and trains him to expect that size for that price.

quiz.prompt: An invoice passed its due date last Friday. The client has always been pleasant, pays eventually, and is clearly busy. Bernard needs the money this month. What should the first message look like?

options.text: Name the invoice and the date it was due, and ask when the payment is scheduled. One question, no apology.
Open by apologising for the bother, mention the invoice, and add that there is no rush on it at all.
Wait another two weeks, since chasing a good client over a single late invoice risks a working relationship.
Say that all further work is on hold until the outstanding invoice has been settled in full on their side.

quiz.explanation: The first ask is written as though it were an oversight, which costs nothing if it turns out not to be. Naming the invoice and the due date and asking one answerable question makes it easy for a busy person to act on. Apologising and saying no rush tells them, accurately, that this can wait, so it does. Waiting longer teaches the client that your dates are soft. Announcing a work stoppage is a second-ask move, and only where a pause was agreed at the start, so using it first turns an administrative miss into a confrontation.

quiz.prompt: Tin has worked with the same client for two years and has decided her rate for this work needs to go up. The relationship is good and nothing is currently on fire. How should she send it?

options.text: A long message setting out rising costs, the new skills she has added, and the extras she absorbs each month.
Mention it in passing on their next call, then let the new figure appear on the invoice that follows it.
A short note with the new rate and the date it takes effect, sent with enough notice for them to plan.
A short note with the new rate, effective immediately, since a long notice period only invites a negotiation.

quiz.explanation: Notice, the figure, the start date, and nothing else. It reads as a business fact and gives the client time to budget, which is what stops it becoming an argument. The long justification is a case the client can dispute point by point. A passing mention on a call is not notice, and a figure that appears unannounced on an invoice feels like a trick. Effective immediately is not notice either, and it removes the one thing that keeps an increase from turning into a negotiation, which is time for the client to plan around it.

modules.title: Complaints, mistakes, and what comes next
modules.description: Repair and renewal. Answering a client who is unhappy, owning a mistake in one sentence rather than five paragraphs, and the messages after a project ends that decide whether there is another one.

lessons.title: Answering an unhappy client
lessons.content_mdx:
# Answering an unhappy client

A message lands at eleven at night. It is from your client and it is not friendly. Your stomach drops, you read it four times, and by the fourth reading you have written a reply in your head that is three paragraphs of apology and one paragraph of explanation.

Put that reply away. This lesson is the one you send instead.

First, the boundary. This is the private complaint aimed at you, about your work, where your own reputation is what is at stake. It is not a public comment thread on a client's page. Answering an angry stranger in front of an audience, while speaking as somebody else's brand, is a different job with different rules, and it belongs to AI Social Media Management.

## Read for the ask, not the tone

An unhappy message carries two things: what happened, and how it was described. Separate them before you type anything.

Rhea, a VA in Bacolod, gets this from her client in Melbourne:

> I have asked twice now for the weekly report and it is still not in the folder. This is exactly the kind of thing that makes me wonder whether this arrangement is working.

The tone puts the whole arrangement in question. The ask is: put the report in the folder. The ask is smaller than the tone, because a person writes at the temperature of the moment they are in, not at the temperature of the problem.

Write the ask down in one line before you reply. Rhea's line: last week's report is not where he expects it. Everything else in that message is weather.

## The shape of the reply

Four parts, in this order.

**Acknowledge the specific thing.** Not the feeling. "Sorry you feel that way" turns one complaint into two, because it tells the reader you have decided their reaction is the problem. Name the actual event: "You asked twice and it was not there. That is on me."

**Say what you will do and when.** A date, not an intention. "The report is in the folder before you start tomorrow, and from now on it goes up every Friday before I sign off."

**Ask one question at the outside, and only if you cannot act without the answer.** Rhea does not need to ask anything. If she genuinely did not know which folder he meant, that is the one question, and it goes at the end.

**Stop.** A long reply reads as an argument even when every sentence in it is true. Short is not curt here. Short is confident.

## Four ways this goes wrong

**You go quiet for a day to calm down.** Silence after a complaint leaves the client guessing, and the guesses are not generous. Send one line as soon as you see it, whatever the hour, and name when the real reply lands: "Reading this properly. Full reply by nine tomorrow morning your time." Then reply by nine. The holding line is what buys you the night. Naming the hour is what makes it a promise rather than a delay.

**You over-apologise.** Past one apology you have handed the client a second job, which is managing your feelings. A client who ends up reassuring you is doing emotional work on top of paying for the job.

**You argue point by point.** Answering all five of their sentences turns the exchange into a debate you can only win by making them wrong. Answer the ask. Correct a factual error once, briefly, and only if it changes what happens next.

**You copy someone in.** Adding the agency owner or a second contact to win the point converts a fixable annoyance into a formal event with witnesses. Bring in another person only when you need a decision that person owns.

## When the complaint is not fair

Sometimes you are being asked to redo work that matches what was agreed, or to absorb a failure that came from something the client controlled. Declining is allowed, and it sounds like this: name what was agreed, name what you can do, and offer the paid route for the rest.

> The revision rounds in the scope are used up. I can do this round as an add-on at my usual rate, or hold it for the next batch. Tell me which you prefer.

No accusation, no defence of your honour, and a decision the client can make in one line.

## When to leave the thread

Move to a call when the same misunderstanding survives two rounds of writing, when the client's messages are getting shorter and colder, or when you need to hear a tone you cannot read on a screen. Keep the call short. End it by saying you will send a recap.

Then send the recap the same day: what you agreed, what you will do, the date. The call repaired the relationship. The recap is what stops the same argument arriving again next month.

## Do this now

Take the last client message that upset you. Write the ask on one line. Then write the four-part reply against that line and nothing else.

lessons.title: When you were actually wrong
lessons.content_mdx:
# When you were actually wrong

Sometimes the complaint is correct. You missed it, you broke it, you sent the wrong file to the wrong list. This lesson is the message you send then, and it is shorter than you think it should be.

## One sentence, then the fix, then stop

The apology that works has three parts and no fourth.

> I sent Tuesday's newsletter to the whole list instead of the lapsed segment. I have paused the follow-up sequence so nothing else goes out, and the corrected send will be ready for your approval before your Wednesday morning, your time. I will send you the segment rules I am working from so you can check I have them right.

Ownership first: one sentence, active voice, you as the subject. "The email went out to the wrong list" is not ownership. "I sent it to the wrong list" is.

Then the fix and the date. Then the thing that stops it repeating, if there is one.

Then stop. No paragraph about how badly you feel. Bad feelings are real, and they are not information the client can use.

## Why your reason does not go in the message

Your connection died. There was a brownout. Traffic on EDSA took three hours out of your day. Someone at home was sick. Every one of those can be completely true, and none of them belongs in the body of this message, because a reason sitting next to a mistake reads as a bid to have the mistake excused, whatever you intended.

Separate a reason from a cause. A cause the client needs in order to decide something goes in, in one clause: "The export failed silently, so I have added a check at the end of the run." That is useful to them. "My internet has been terrible all week" is not, because there is nothing they can do with it.

There is one exception, and it is about capacity rather than about this mistake. If something in your life is going to affect the next two weeks of work, that is its own message, sent on purpose, saying what you can still commit to. It is not a footnote to an apology.

## What to offer

Offer the fix. Offer the date. If the mistake cost the client something concrete, offer the specific thing that restores it: the redo, the extra pass, the hours you will not bill.

Do not volunteer a discount before anyone asks for one, and do not offer to work free for an unnamed stretch of time. A large unprompted offer tells the client the mistake was bigger than they had understood, and it sets the price of every future mistake.

## Stop apologising on a schedule

You apologise once, properly. Then you do the work.

The temptation over the following weeks is to keep referring back to it. "Again, so sorry about the newsletter." Every mention reopens something the client had already filed away, and asks them to reassure you again. After the first apology, let the fix be the apology.

What does belong in those weeks is short-term over-communication with an end date you say out loud: "For the next three sends I will ping you before each one goes out, then we can go back to the normal Friday update." Naming the end date is what makes it read as a repair rather than as a permanent state of anxiety.

## The disclosure call

The harder judgment is not how to apologise. It is whether to say anything at all.

Fix quietly: a typo you catch before the client sees it, a wrong file you replace within minutes, a formula you corrected while the number was still yours alone. Work in progress does not need a bulletin.

Disclose even when nobody would have noticed: anything that leaves the client holding something untrue, anything touching money, anything a third party has already seen, anything that will look like concealment when it surfaces later.

One question decides it. If this comes out in a month, does it look like a mistake, or does it look like a cover-up? A wrong figure in a report you already sent gets disclosed even if the client will never recompute it, because on the day they do recompute it you stop being a person who erred and become a person who knew.

Marisol, a bookkeeping VA in Dumaguete, found she had filed a client's supplier payments under the wrong heading for a whole month. Nobody had asked. She sent one line naming the error, one line on the fix and the date it would be done, and one line on the check she had added. She does not know what the client thought of it. What she knows is that the correction was hers to make, and that it was never going to get cheaper than it was that morning.

## Do this now

Write your last mistake as one sentence with you as the subject. Then delete the reason.

lessons.title: The messages that bring the next job
lessons.content_mdx:
# The messages that bring the next job

A project ends. You send "thank you so much, it was a pleasure working with you," and then nothing. Four months later you are pitching strangers again, while a client who liked your work has quietly hired somebody else, because you never told them you were available.

The end of a project is a writing problem, and it is the cheapest one in this course to fix.

## The handover message

Send it the day you deliver, not the week after.

What a handover has to contain, and the order the files and the account access move in, is Project and Client Operations' subject. This is the message that carries it, and two of its lines are pure wording.

**What you will still answer, and for how long.** "I will answer anything about this handover for the next two weeks at no charge." Naming the window is what stops a year of unpaid support requests, and it also stops the client feeling dropped. Help with no end date on it is not generosity. It is an invoice neither of you can see.

**What comes next, if anything.** One line: "If you want me to run the monthly refresh, tell me by the end of the month and I will hold the slot."

That last line is the difference between a project that ends and a client who continues. It is not a pitch. It is a door left open with a handle on it.

## The check-in to a quiet client

Three months of silence, and you want to ask whether there is work. The instinct is to open by apologising for disturbing them, which announces that you consider yourself a nuisance before they have decided anything.

Be specific instead. A check-in works when it carries something.

> Hi Ram, the product pages we rewrote in March are due for their seasonal update, and I have capacity in the first half of next month. Want me to take a pass? If the timing is wrong, no problem, I will check back after the holidays.

Specific work, specific timing, an easy no. Send it once, note the date you sent it, and let it rest. What you never send: "Just checking in!" with nothing attached.

## Asking for a testimonial

People agree to help and then do not, because you handed them homework. Remove the homework. Name the specific work, say where it goes, and offer to draft something they can change.

> Would you be willing to leave two or three lines about the inventory tracker for my profile? Happy to draft something you can edit or rewrite completely.

When to ask, and how to describe the next client you want, are Project and Client Operations' subject. The wording is what this lesson owns: a named piece of work, a length, and an offer to write the first version yourself.

## The client who ended badly

Some engagements end on a missed date, an argument, or a month where you were not good. Those clients are the ones nobody ever writes to, which is exactly why a message from you is worth something.

Write it once and keep it short. Name the thing without excavating it, report what changed, and ask for nothing.

> Hi Dana, the reporting was late twice at the end of last year and I know that made your month harder. I moved that work to a fixed Friday slot and it has held since. If you ever want another pair of hands on it, I am here. Either way, no reply needed.

It names the actual failure, so she does not have to wonder whether you noticed. It reports a change rather than an intention, which is the only kind of apology worth anything a year late. And it closes the exit, so reading it costs her nothing. Do not attach a rate or a calendar link: a pitch from the person who let you down reads as though the apology was only the wrapper.

## When they ask for a discount to renew

Renewal is where a client asks for a lower number, because your work is already in hand and the leverage feels like theirs. The answer is the one from chapter 3: move the work, not the rate.

> I would rather not drop the rate for the same scope. What I can do is take the weekly report to fortnightly, which brings the monthly figure to about where you want it. The other option is that everything stays as it is. Both work for me.

No wounded paragraph, no threat to leave, two real options. If they hold at a number you cannot work for, say so plainly and name your last date.

## Ending it on purpose

If a rate change is due, it goes out on its own and ahead of the invoice that carries it, never attached to it. The wording is in chapter 3.

Ending a client relationship on purpose is the message freelancers avoid until avoiding it turns into ghosting. Name the last date you will work, hand everything over, and say nothing about why unless there is something the client can act on.

> I am winding down this type of work, and my last week with you will be the week of the fifteenth. Everything is in the handover doc, including the two recurring tasks and where the templates live. Happy to answer questions from whoever picks it up.

Notice what is not in it. No grievances, no account of what they did, no invitation to talk you out of it. A reason the client cannot act on is a parting shot dressed as feedback, and it is the part they will remember and repeat.

Give more notice than feels comfortable, and put it in writing before you say it on a call. A client told in March can hire in April. And protect the person who comes after you: your replacement reads that handover, and the client remembers whether the freelancer who left them left them a mess.

## Do this now

Pick one client whose project ended and who never heard from you again. Write the specific check-in for them, with the work named and the timing named. Send it or do not, but write it.

quiz.prompt: Rhea, a VA in Bacolod, opens this at eleven at night from her client in Melbourne: "I've asked twice now about the invoice run and it still has not gone out. This is exactly the kind of thing that makes me wonder whether this arrangement is working." She checks and he is right, she forgot it. Which reply should she send?

options.text: You asked twice and it did not go out. That is on me. The invoices go before you start tomorrow, and the run moves to a fixed Friday slot.
I am so sorry you feel that way about how this has been going. I never meant to make you feel unsupported, and I promise I will do much better.
Apologies for the delay. To explain, I did have the invoices ready, but the billing tool has been unreliable all week, which I did flag earlier.
Sorry about that! Let me look into what happened over the last two weeks and I will come back to you once I work out where it went.

quiz.explanation: The ask is smaller than the tone: get the invoices out. Option a names the specific event, takes ownership, and gives a time the client can hold her to, anchored to his morning rather than to her night. Option b answers the feeling instead of the event, which is the reply that turns one complaint into two. Option c is a reason placed next to a mistake, which reads as a bid to be excused. Option d promises to investigate something Rhea already knows the answer to.

quiz.prompt: Ben, a freelance designer in Cebu, gets a long unhappy message from a client at four in the afternoon. Reading it makes his hands shake and he knows anything he writes right now will be five paragraphs of apology. What should he do?

options.text: Reply immediately with a full apology and a promise to fix it, before checking what actually happened.
Wait until morning, when he can answer calmly and the client will be awake to read it anyway.
Send one line now naming the hour the full reply will land, then send the full reply at that hour.
Forward the thread to the agency owner who introduced them, so somebody senior can settle the client down.

quiz.explanation: Silence after a complaint leaves the client guessing, and the guesses are not generous, so the overnight gap in option b costs more than the calm it buys. What buys the calm without the silence is a holding line with an hour named in it: the client stops guessing, and Ben still gets the time he needs. Option a sends an apology before Ben knows what he is apologising for. Option d converts an annoyance into a formal event with witnesses. A holding line only works if the real reply arrives at the hour it promised.

quiz.prompt: Kim's scope with a Sydney client included a set number of revision rounds. They are used up, and the client has just sent a fourth round of changes with no mention of the limit. What should Kim write?

options.text: Do the revision without mentioning it, since arguing over one round is not worth risking a good client for.
Say the agreed rounds are used up, offer this round as an add-on at her usual rate or in the next batch, and let the client pick.
Explain in detail how each earlier round was used up, listing every change the client requested and the date on which each one arrived.
Decline the request and point out that the scope was agreed in writing before any of the work on the project started.

quiz.explanation: Declining is allowed, and it works when it names what was agreed, names what you can do, and hands back a decision. Option a makes the limit invisible, so the fifth round arrives too. Option c relitigates history the client did not dispute. Option d refuses without offering a route, which leaves the client stuck and looking for someone else.

quiz.prompt: Two weeks after sending a monthly report, Joan finds a figure in it was calculated on the wrong column. The client has not queried it and probably never will. Nothing in the client's decisions has changed because of it. What should she do?

options.text: Fix it quietly in the next report, since correcting a figure nobody queried only draws attention to a mistake that caused no harm at all.
Mention it at the bottom of the next weekly update, under the other items, so it is on the record without becoming the headline of the week.
Wait to see whether the client raises it, and keep a clear explanation ready to send in case they ever do.
Tell them today in one line, give the corrected figure, and name the check she has added so it cannot happen again.

quiz.explanation: The test is what it looks like if it surfaces in a month. The client is holding a number that is not true, so this is disclosed even though nobody would have noticed. Options a and c both rely on it never coming up, and on the day it does she stops being a person who erred and becomes a person who knew. Option b buries a wrong figure under routine items.

quiz.prompt: A brownout in Iloilo cost Arvin an afternoon and he missed a delivery time he had promised. The work will now land the next morning. He is writing the message. What goes in it?

options.text: Own the miss in one sentence, name the exact time the work will now land, and keep the brownout out of the message entirely.
Explain the brownout early so the client understands the cause was outside his control, then give the new time.
Apologise at length, describe the power situation in detail, and offer to take something off the invoice to make up for it.
Send the work late with no comment, on the grounds that a short delay nobody has asked about needs no announcement.

quiz.explanation: The brownout is true and it is still not information the client can use, so next to the mistake it reads as a bid to be excused. Option c adds an unprompted discount, which tells the client the mistake was bigger than they thought and prices every future one. Option d is the silence that turns a small slip into a trust problem.

quiz.prompt: Three months after redesigning the menus for a bakery in Iloilo, Fatima wants more work from them. They parted on good terms and she has capacity next month. Which message should she send?

options.text: "Hi Nel! Just checking in and hoping all is well over there. Let me know if you need anything at all, anytime."
"Hi Nel, sorry to bother you. I know you are busy. If you ever have spare work I would really appreciate it."
"Hi Nel, the menus need a Christmas version and I have capacity next month. Want a pass? No problem if not."
"Hi Nel, work has been quiet on my side this quarter, so I wanted to ask whether there is anything you could send my way."

quiz.explanation: A check-in works when it carries something: specific work, specific timing, and an easy no. Option a gives Nel nothing to react to. Option b opens by announcing she considers herself a nuisance. Option d makes her situation the reason to hire her, which asks the client to do her a favour rather than to buy something useful.

quiz.prompt: Marj is writing the handover message on a website build. She wants to stay genuinely helpful without being on call for a year. Which line does that?

options.text: "Message me any time at all if something comes up with the site. I am always happy to help you out."
"Any support after today is chargeable, so send over whatever comes up and I will quote it for you first."
"Everything you need is in the handover document, so you should not run into anything at all after today."
"I will answer anything about this handover free for two weeks. After that it is a job we can price."

quiz.explanation: Naming the window is what stops a year of unpaid support requests, and it also stops the client feeling dropped. Option a sounds generous and is an invoice neither of you can see, because it has no end and no price on it. Option b puts a meter on the client the day they take delivery, which reads as the door closing behind the invoice. Option c is a prediction nobody can make about somebody else's website, and it is the sentence they will quote back the first time something breaks.

quiz.prompt: Charmaine is winding down VA work to take a full-time job. One client is left, and she runs two recurring tasks nobody else in that business knows how to do. How should she close it?

options.text: Tell the client she is leaving and offer to keep running the two recurring tasks free until they replace her.
Name her last working date now, hand over the two recurring tasks and the templates, and offer to answer whoever replaces her.
Tell the client she is leaving and explain in full why the arrangement stopped working for her, so they can do better with the next VA.
Finish out the month, then send a short goodbye saying it was a pleasure, without going into recurring tasks nobody has asked about.

quiz.explanation: Ending on purpose means a last date, a real handover, and no commentary the client cannot act on. Option a ends the arrangement and then does not end it: an unpaid commitment with no last date on it is how a wind-down turns into another six months, and the tasks stay undocumented the whole time. Option c hands over a critique instead of instructions. Option d leaves two undocumented tasks to fail after she is gone, and the client remembers who left them the mess.

assignment.title: Five messages, one bad week
assignment.brief_mdx:
You write five real messages to one client, against the week described below. The week is fixed. The work is yours.

**Set your own three lines first.** Open your submission with what you do for this client, what you are currently delivering, and the day you send your weekly update. Use your own trade, whether that is design, admin, bookkeeping, writing, video or support. If you have no client yet, use the work you are training for and a client you can picture.

**The week.** The engagement has been running for a couple of months. The client runs a small business in another country, writes in short lines, and rarely uses a greeting. Then:

- **Tuesday.** The client sends a screenshot and one sentence: "Can you do this one too? Should be quick." It is real work, it was never in what you agreed, and it is not quick.
- **Wednesday morning.** You can see that the main thing due Friday will not be ready until the middle of next week. Part of that is your own misjudgment. Part of it is a file you asked them for last week and still do not have.
- **Wednesday afternoon.** You hit a decision you cannot make for them. There are two ways to finish the remaining piece: one faster and thinner, one slower and complete.
- **Thursday.** The client replies to something you delivered a week ago. They say it was not what they asked for, they fixed it themselves, and they want to know why they had to find that out on their own.
- **Friday.** Your update is due, and this was a week where almost nothing got finished.

**Write the five messages, in the order they are sent.** Label each with its day. Roughly 800 to 1,000 words in total, so none of them is long. Write them as the client would receive them, not as a description of what you would say.

1. **Tuesday, the extra request.** Answer "can you do this one too" so that both the relationship and the scope survive. Name what the request changes: the date, the cost, or what gets dropped instead. Do not quote a figure. If cost is the honest answer, say that it changes the cost and that you will send the number separately.
2. **Wednesday, the delay.** Sent the day you see it, not on Friday. What happened, what it does to their date, what you are already doing about it, and what they need to decide.
3. **Wednesday, the question.** One message, one decision, answerable in a line. Give only the context needed to choose, name your recommendation, and name the default you will proceed with if you have not heard back by a day you state.
4. **Thursday, the complaint.** Reply to the unhappy message. Acknowledge the specific thing that went wrong. Say what you will do and by when. Ask at most one clarifying question. Keep it short.
5. **Friday, the update.** The standing update for a week that went badly: what is done, what is in progress, what is blocked and who it is waiting on, what is next. It comes last on purpose. Nothing in it may be the first time the client hears bad news, and nothing in it may be padded to look busier than the week was.

**Then a closing note, four or five lines.** Quote the most apologetic sentence you wrote in your own first draft, then the sentence you replaced it with, and say in one line what changed.

Plain text or Markdown. Change or remove real client names and business details before you submit. Do not state a rate, a fee, a platform commission, a tax rule or a named app screen anywhere in this: if an honest message needs a number you do not have, say you will confirm it and send it.
criteria: All seven parts are present against one situation: the three setup lines, five separate messages labelled with the day they are sent, and the closing note. The same project, deliverable and dates run through all five messages

Every message opens with the answer or the point in its first line rather than an apology, a wind-up or a greeting paragraph, asks the client for one thing at most, and states no rate, fee, platform commission, tax rule or named app screen the learner would have to invent

The Friday update carries the bad week in a fixed shape: what is done, what is in progress, what is blocked and who it is waiting on, what is next. It hides nothing, repeats nothing as news that was already sent earlier in the week, and is short enough to read on a phone
The Tuesday reply names what the extra request changes in time, in cost, or in what gets dropped instead, and leaves the client a decision to make. It is neither a flat refusal nor a silent yes

The Wednesday delay message is sent on Wednesday and says what happened, what it does to the client's date, and what the client has to decide. It is not buried inside other news and it promises no recovery the writer could not actually make

The Wednesday question can be answered in one line: one decision, only the context needed to make it, a named recommendation, and a default with a stated day that falls before the writer is forced to act
The Thursday reply acknowledges the specific complaint, gives a remedy with a date, and neither grovels nor argues point by point
